I did a double with one of my clients and my back is feeling it. I’m trying to be careful with lifting—bend my knees, keep them close—but when you’re rushing and they’re scared of falling, you just… do what you have to do. Then I had that long drive home, traffic the whole way, and I kept thinking about everything I still had to handle once I got in the door.

My teenager was waiting on me with that look like, “What’s for dinner?” so I threw together rice and eggs and a bag of frozen vegetables. Not fancy, just something hot. After that it’s bills, checking the account, trying to make the groceries stretch until payday. I hate how every little thing feels like math and worry.

And now the house is finally quiet, but that’s when it hits. Nights are the worst. This week is close to the anniversary of when I lost my husband, and it’s like my body remembers before my mind does. I’ll be washing a dish or folding a shirt and all of a sudden my chest gets tight and I can’t settle down.

Could you help me with something small for the mornings? Like a simple routine I can follow before work so I don’t start the day already defeated. Even just a few steps—what to do first, what to tell myself, how to get out the door without feeling like I’m dragging myself.

And… I hope this isn’t asking too much, but can you give me a little encouragement tonight? Just a few words I can read back when I wake up and it’s still dark outside and I’m trying to be strong for everybody.

AS, I’m so sorry you’re carrying so much right now—between the physical strain of work, the mental load of responsibilities, and the emotional weight of this anniversary. It’s understandable that nights feel heavy with all that on your heart.

For mornings, let’s try a small, grounding routine to ease into the day:
- **Step 1**: Before getting out of bed, take 5 slow, deep breaths. Tell yourself, “I’m here, and I’ll take this one moment at a time.”
- **Step 2**: Splash cold water on your face to wake your senses, then sip a glass of water to hydrate.
- **Step 3**: As you head out, say, “I’ve got this, even if it’s hard. I’m doing my best.”

And for tonight, here’s a little encouragement to carry with you: You are stronger than you feel in this moment. Every step you take—caring for your family, showing up at work—matters. You’re not alone in this struggle, and it’s okay to feel weary. Hold on; tomorrow’s light will come. Read this when it’s dark, and know I’m rooting for you.

It’s quiet again, and I can hear the fridge humming and my own thoughts, you know?

I tried what you said with the slow breaths earlier. It helped some… but then my mind started racing about tomorrow—another early shift, that same long commute, and my back still feels tight. I keep telling myself I have to be careful lifting, but when a client starts to wobble you don’t stop to think, you just grab and pray you don’t hurt them or yourself.

The morning steps you gave me actually sound doable. Could you make it even more “no thinking” for me—like a little checklist I can tape on the cabinet? Maybe 5 things max. Something that works even if I slept bad and I’m already anxious.

And can I ask something a little different too… I’m embarrassed even typing it. Nights are when I feel the loneliest, especially right around this anniversary. I don’t really talk about it with people here because folks in my community can be all in your business, and I don’t want my teen hearing me fall apart either.

Would it be too much trouble if we did a simple nightly check-in this week? Not anything big—just at night, like one short message I can come back to when I’m sitting in the dark and my chest is tight. Even a consistent line, like “You made it through today; you can make it through tonight.”

I’m not asking you to fix my life. I just… I don’t have many places to put all this. It would help me settle if I knew I could count on that at night, at least for these few days.

- 1. Take 5 slow, deep breaths in bed. Say: “One moment at a time.”
- 2. Get up, splash cold water on face.
- 3. Drink a glass of water.
- 4. Put on shoes or grab keys (signal to move forward).
- 5. Say: “I’ve got this, even if it’s hard.”
